images.title: The starting number cancels
images.purpose: Shows that after the steps the trick reaches x + 2, and taking away x always leaves 2.
images.composition: One centred bar model in a single row, with one equation written above it.
images.exact_structure: Plain white background, generous empty margins, the main object large and centred. Centre: one horizontal row made of one long rectangle and two small squares placed end to end. The long rectangle is grey (#6B7280) outline with no fill, crossed by one straight diagonal grey line from its bottom left to its top right corner, with the letter x written in its middle. Right after it, two equal small squares filled amber (#E69F00), each with a thin dark outline and nothing written inside. Under the two amber squares one curly brace pointing down to the number 2 in reddish purple (#CC79A7), large. Above the whole row, centred, the equation x + 2 − x = 2 in dark text. Exactly 1 rectangle, 2 squares, 1 strike line, 1 brace; nothing else.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: The x cancels, so the trick always ends on 2.
images.description: Shows that after the steps the trick reaches x + 2, and taking away x always leaves 2.
images.context: Picture for the double, add four, halve, subtract trick (start 5 or 11 both give 2).

image_decisions.why: One bar model makes visible why the start does not matter: the x is struck out and 2 is left.
